hints: Start by tracing the direction of an impulse in a sensory neurone - it begins at a receptor and travels toward the central nervous system, so look at the far left and far right ends of Fig. 1.1.
Remember a sensory neurone has a short dendron leading from the receptor to the cell body, and a long axon leading away - the dendron is the first thin fibre after the receptor cells.
Think about which covering around the fibre speeds up impulses by insulating it, and where gaps in that covering allow depolarisation to happen.
Recall that the branched endings at the far end of the neurone form synapses with the next neurone in the pathway, the intermediate neurone.
walkthrough:
Map the sensory pathway from left to right**
Think of a sensory neurone as a messenger carrying information inward. On the left you have the cells that detect a stimulus. These are the receptor cells, labelled A. Their membranes generate a receptor potential which triggers an impulse in the adjoining dendron.

Separate dendron from axon using the cell body**
The cell body D sits in the middle. The short fibre to the left of D connecting to the receptors is the dendron. The long fibre to the right of D going toward the CNS is the axon. Depolarisation during an action potential occurs at exposed membrane. Label C points to a node between Schwann cells on the dendron side, so C is an area where dendron membrane depolarisation occurs.

Identify insulation for fast conduction**
Label B points to a Schwann cell forming the myelin sheath. Myelin is fatty insulation that prevents ion movement across the membrane underneath it. This forces depolarisation to jump from node to node by saltatory conduction, greatly increasing speed. So B allows rapid transmission.

Find the output end**
Label F shows the fine branched synaptic terminals at the end of the axon. These swellings contain vesicles of transmitter and form synapses with the intermediate neurone in the spinal cord or brain. So F is the structure that forms a synapse with an intermediate neurone.

Final answer: receptor cell - A; area where dendron membrane depolarisation occurs - C; structure that forms a synapse with an intermediate neurone - F; structure that allows rapid transmission of impulses - B.

hints: Look carefully at Fig. 1.2 and follow the arrows - when the opioid drug binds, the G protein is activated and then does something to the channel protein on the right.
Remind yourself what normally has to enter the presynaptic knob when an action potential arrives, and what that ion does to vesicles inside.
Think about how the amount of transmitter released into the cleft controls how much binds on the other side - less release means less binding.
Link events on the postsynaptic membrane to the final outcome - what ion movement causes depolarisation and what happens if threshold is not reached.
walkthrough:
Start with the block shown in Fig. 1.2**
When opioid drug binds its receptor, the G protein is activated and causes blockage of the voltage-gated $Ca^{2+}$ channel protein. Even when an action potential arrives at the presynaptic knob, no or less $Ca^{2+}$ can enter the cytoplasm through the presynaptic membrane.

Link calcium to vesicle release**
In a normal cholinergic synapse, $Ca^{2+}$ influx causes vesicles containing acetylcholine (ACh) to move to, fuse with and release by exocytosis at the presynaptic membrane. With $Ca^{2+}$ channels blocked, no or less fusion and exocytosis occurs, so no or less ACh is released into the synaptic cleft.

Follow ACh across the cleft**
Normally diffusing ACh binds to nicotinic cholinergic receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening chemically-gated $Na^{+}$ channels. With less ACh released, no or less ACh binds to receptors, so fewer $Na^{+}$ channels open.

Finish with the postsynaptic response**
Less $Na^{+}$ entry means no or less depolarisation of the postsynaptic membrane, so the generator potential does not reach threshold. This results in no or fewer action potentials in the postsynaptic neurone, so transmission is inhibited and pain signalling is reduced.

Final answer: Opioid inhibits transmission: no / less $Ca^{2+}$ enter presynaptic knob; no / less vesicles fuse with presynaptic membrane / release acetylcholine by exocytosis; no / less acetylcholine binds to receptors on postsynaptic membrane; no / less $Na^{+}$ enter postsynaptic neurone / no / less depolarisation; no / fewer action potentials in postsynaptic neurone.
